blocks.text: — — — nor the rock, or the punishment of the black vulture. — — — — — —
With his dug-out entrails he feeds the black birds.
Black birds, that is, black vultures. Physicians, too, prefer to use the black vulture in their remedies. Thus Samonicus, in chapter 14, would have applied, to soothe pain of the eyes,
— — — — the gall of the black vulture, with which blades of celandine have been mixed.
And in chapter 34, πρὸς εὐτοκίαν [pros eutokian] [for an easy delivery]:
— — they place beneath the dung of the black vulture, so that she may scarcely feel the birth that presses close. [II, 786] And in chapter 58, for the falling sickness:
The gall of the black vulture is of help with old Bacchus.

Others, however, read ampli [large]; and Pliny makes an exception for remedies against serpents, in which, he writes in book 29, chapter 4, black vultures are less effective. Among birds (he says) the vulture is foremost as a help against serpents. It has also been noted that the black ones have less power. That those black vultures are properly called αἰγυπιοὺς [aigypious], that they are of both sexes, unlike other vultures, and that they stand between the eagle kind and the vulture kind, Aelian reports in book 2, chapter 46, in these words: Τοὺς δὲ αἰγυπιοὺς (λέγουσιν) ἐν μεθορίῳ γυπῶν ὄντας καὶ αἰετῶν, εἶναι καὶ ἄῤῥενας, καὶ τὴν χρόαν πεφυκέναι μέλανας [tous de aigypious (legousin) en methoriō gypōn ontas kai aietōn, einai kai arrhenas, kai tēn chroan pephykenai melanas]. And Philes hints that aegypii are so called for Aegyptii [Egyptians], when he writes in chapter 2: εἶναι δὲ καὶ τοὺς μέλανας ὡς Αἰγυπτίους [einai de kai tous melanas hōs Aigyptious], that they too are black, like Egyptians^{(4)}. But αἰγυπιὸς [aigypios] is one thing, Αἰγύπτιος [Aigyptios] another. The former comes from γυπός [gypos]; the latter is formed from Cophti.
